checklistItems.label: Complete the online application form
checklistItems.tip: Use exactly the same name spelling as on your passport or national ID.

checklistItems.label: Academic transcripts / results slips
checklistItems.tip: Request certified copies early — schools can take 1–3 weeks.

checklistItems.label: Certificates (e.g. UCE/UACE, KCSE, WASSCE)
checklistItems.tip: If results are pending, most universities accept provisional results first.

checklistItems.label: National ID or passport copy
checklistItems.tip: Scan in colour, all four corners visible.

checklistItems.label: Personal statement / motivation letter
checklistItems.tip: Write it in the Statement Studio — it checks length and clichés for you.

checklistItems.label: Pay the application fee (official channel only)
checklistItems.tip: Pay only through the university's official portal or bank account. Keep the receipt.

checklistItems.label: Birth certificate
checklistItems.tip: Some public universities ask for it at registration.

checklistItems.label: Check government sponsorship / loan eligibility
checklistItems.tip: Compare merit, district quota and student-loan options before paying privately.

checklistItems.label: Valid passport
checklistItems.tip: Ideally valid for your whole planned stay. Renewals can take weeks.

checklistItems.label: English test results (IELTS/TOEFL/Duolingo) or waiver
checklistItems.tip: Many universities waive tests for English-medium schooling — ask for a waiver letter.

checklistItems.label: Recommendation letters
checklistItems.tip: Ask referees at least 4–6 weeks before the deadline. Use the Reference Kit.

checklistItems.label: Proof of funds / bank statement
checklistItems.tip: Usually needed for the visa; check the exact amount and how recent it must be.

checklistItems.label: Check qualification equivalency
checklistItems.tip: Confirm whether your certificate needs a foundation year or credential evaluation.

checklistItems.label: Research visa / study permit requirements
checklistItems.tip: Look up the official immigration website for your destination country.

checklistItems.label: Academic CV
checklistItems.tip: Two pages max. Lead with education, research and relevant work.

checklistItems.label: Degree certificate and transcript
checklistItems.tip: If you haven't graduated yet, a provisional transcript is usually fine.

checklistItems.label: Statement of purpose or research proposal
checklistItems.tip: Connect your past work to what you'll study and what you'll do after.

glossary.definition: An offer of admission that becomes final only after you meet stated conditions, such as final exam results or an English test score.
An offer with no academic conditions left to meet. You may still need to accept, pay a deposit, or register by a deadline.
A short essay explaining why you want to study the course, what prepared you, and what you hope to do next.
The postgraduate version of a personal statement — more focused on academic interests, research and career plans.
An official record of the subjects you took and the grades you earned, issued by your school or university.
In Uganda's UACE, a pass at A-level standard (grades A–E) in a principal subject. Universities usually ask for at least two.
How your certificate compares to the entry requirements of another country's system. Some countries require a foundation year.
A one-year preparatory programme that bridges your secondary qualification to a degree in another education system.
A payment some universities request to hold your place. Pay only through official university channels.
Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies — a reference number a UK university gives you to apply for a Student visa.
A US form issued by your university that you need to apply for an F-1 student visa.
Permission to study in a country such as Canada. Usually requires an acceptance letter and proof of funds.
A bank account (common for Germany) holding a fixed amount you can withdraw monthly — used as proof of funds for a visa.
Applications are reviewed as they arrive until places fill, so applying early improves your chances.
Permission to apply without paying the application fee — often available for students with financial need. Always ask.
The month a programme starts (e.g. August or January). Some universities have more than one intake per year.

faqs.a: Yes. Discovering programmes, matching, checklists, the document vault, the tracker and all preparation tools are free. In future we may offer optional paid human support — core guidance will stay free.

faqs.q: Does a match mean I will be admitted?
faqs.a: No. A match shows programmes that appear to fit your results, budget and goals based on published requirements. Universities make all admission decisions.

When you create a free account, your profile, applications and documents are stored securely on UniPath’s servers so you can use any device and our advisers can help you. Without an account, everything stays only on the device you’re using. You can download or delete your data at any time.

faqs.q: Can I apply directly through UniPath?
faqs.a: Not yet. We link you to each university's official application portal and help you prepare and track everything. Direct submission will come with university partnerships.

faqs.q: Do universities pay to appear higher?
faqs.a: No. Matches are ranked only by how well a programme fits you. Any future partnership will be clearly disclosed.

faqs.q: How accurate are fees and deadlines?
faqs.a: Figures marked 'Indicative' are estimates. Programmes marked 'Verified' have been checked against the official website on the date shown. Always confirm on the official site before paying anything.

faqs.q: I don't have my final results yet. Can I still use it?
faqs.a: Yes. Use your predicted or mock results. Many universities accept applications before final results and make a conditional offer.

faqs.q: Can I use it on my phone with poor internet?
faqs.a: Yes. UniPath works on any phone browser and keeps working offline once loaded. You can also add it to your home screen like an app.

enrollSteps.title: Understand your offer
enrollSteps.detail: Is it conditional or unconditional? Note every condition, the acceptance deadline and any deposit required.

enrollSteps.title: Compare offers and costs
enrollSteps.detail: Use the Cost Planner to compare the full cost of each offer, including living costs and scholarships.

enrollSteps.title: Accept your chosen offer
enrollSteps.detail: Accept through the official portal before the deadline. Politely decline the others so places go to other students.

enrollSteps.title: Pay deposit or fees — safely
enrollSteps.detail: Use only the bank details printed on the official offer letter or portal. Never pay an agent's personal account.

enrollSteps.title: Confirm funding
enrollSteps.detail: Get written confirmation of any scholarship, sponsorship or loan, and know when funds are released.

enrollSteps.title: Arrange accommodation
enrollSteps.detail: Apply for university housing early, or research verified private hostels close to campus.

enrollSteps.title: Visa or study permit (if studying abroad)
enrollSteps.detail: Gather your CAS/I-20/acceptance letter, proof of funds and passport, then apply on the official government website.

enrollSteps.title: Health checks and insurance
enrollSteps.detail: Complete any medical forms, vaccinations and health insurance the university or visa requires.

enrollSteps.title: Plan travel and arrival
enrollSteps.detail: Book travel after your visa is approved. Note orientation dates and airport pick-up options.

enrollSteps.title: Register and attend orientation
enrollSteps.detail: Bring original documents for verification, complete registration, and get your student ID.
